content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach to denoise noisy speech signals by modeling the noise explicitly. The authors claim that instead of modeling speaker(s), modeling the noise helps obtain a unified speaker-independent denoiser. In addition, a large-scale noise dataset, AudioNoiseSet, derived from Audioset dataset is also proposed. Experiments are done using the dataset generated (mixed) by the authors.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The model framework to apply noise information for SE is quite interesting. The authors also bring up an interesting topic that modeling speech explicitly may not be optimal (e.g., language dependent, etc.).

However, I’m not totally convinced by this opinion, because (as shown in Fig.1) if a model can extract the noise from noisy speech, very likely, it can also extract speech from noisy speech. In addition, there are many missing details in the experiment to verify modeling noise is better than modeling speech. Although the results of “Denoiser Only” is reported, it is quite unclear of the detailed model structure and training method/loss. The authors can plot another framework in the appendix for “Denoiser Only” as it is very critical to show that under a fair comparison, modeling noise is really better than modeling speech. In addition, I believe it is unfair to compare the proposed method with the pre-trained SOTA directly because the training dataset is different (i.e., as pointed out by the authors, AVSPEECH contains a variety of languages covering different accents and speaking styles). I strongly encourage the authors to train the proposed model using the same training set (e.g., VCTK) and report the results as those used in the original papers of SOTA. In summary, the experiments do not provide convincing evidence and many details are missing, hence it is difficult to draw conclusions. Other comments are listed as follows:

1) Figure 1 is very confusing. Because the authors claimed that this is a two-step training framework, it should not be plotted in the same figure (i.e., the noise-only model should be plotted separately).
2) I’m not sure why e.q.(4) can help the training, how do you ensure the clean features (Ac) learned by the teacher model and the estimated clean features are in the same embedding space? Do the two BLSTM models share weights in fig. 1?
3) It is well-known that pesq and stoi may not reflect the true quality of the speech generated by a vocoder. It is better to also report other scores such as DNSMOS.
4) There are several problems in section 5 (user study). First, there is no caption for the two figures shown on page 9. Second, in the two figures, it is quite unclear whether you compare your method with ‘VoiceFixer’ or ‘your method by VoiceFixer post-processed'. Third, VoiceFixer is a relatively weak baseline in Tables 2 and 3, you should compare your method with LSS. Fourth, you mentioned “mixed audio, the reconstruction from the base network (first), and our enhanced prediction (second)”, for a fair subjective test, you should randomize the order of the  “base network” and “our enhanced prediction”.
5) Details about the model structure used in the proposed framework are missing.

Typos:
1) Page 3, no citation for VQVAE.
2) In section 4.2, Tab 7. -> Tab. 1.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea of modeling noise for speech enhancement is not very novel. However, the model framework (e.g., VQ-VAE, cross attention, and vocoder, etc) to apply noise information for SE is quite novel. Because there are many details missing about the model structure, it may be hard to reproduce the results by readers.
content.summary_of_the_review: Because it is difficult to see if the proposed method really outperforms the traditional methods in the experiments (e.g., unclear about the (baseline) performance by modeling speech, fairness of comparing with SOTA, and issues in user study), I would recommend rejection for this paper.

content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new method for denoising noisy speech by learning a feature representation of the underlying noise source. It uses a feature disentanglement block to separate out features belonging to speech and noise, and then generates a mel-spectrogram of the clean speech which is converted back into the time domain.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
Although this isn't the first paper to try to model the noise for speech denoising, the method itself is interesting and models the information flow in an intuitive way. Overall, I thought the method was interesting. I'm not sure whether modeling the output as melspectrogram + vocoding is better than trying to generate a raw waveform directly.

Weaknesses:
The experimental section is not rigorous and thorough. In a well studied field like speech enhancement, clear experiments are crucial for establishing the significance of the method.

Firstly, the results qualitatively are not too impressive. Even at moderate noise levels, the output voice is robotic and distorted. I am very familiar with some of the baseline methods (e.g. Segan, Denoiser by Defossez et. al) and it seems surprising to me that this method is outperforming them. It is normal to include the output samples from the baseline methods in the supplementary materials for the reviewer to hear and compare, but only the samples from LSS were included.

It seems unreasonable to use the pretrained models from the baseline methods on the test set of this specific dataset which "Ours" was trained on. Given the distribution of the dataset, it would be necessary to train the baseline methods on the same training set. This is not too unreasonable, and many of these baseline methods have easily reproducible training code.

Finally, this method is only demonstrated on synthetic mixtures of noise + speech from these datasets and not on real data. If the method could generalize, then the authors should show an example of an in-the-wild scenario. If the method doesn't generalize then that is something to point out. For example, the noise and speech samples were recorded in different environments, so the network may be picking up on reverb difference, microphone frequency differences, or any other differences in distribution that would be present between the noise and speech datasets. Normally the user study would be done on in-the-wild data because there is no ground truth available. Such a user study would provide compelling evidence that this method outperforms the baseline methods.

Some questions below:
The notation in the formulation where a is the mixed signal and a_i is the source signal is confusing. Since there is only one source signal, why is it a_i?

Both PESQ and STOI also require fairly strict sample level alignment. If those are possible then wouldn't SDR and SNR also be possible?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a method for speech denoising based on noise modeling instead of speech modeling. This approach is in a sense orthogonal to standard approaches that model speech. The method articulates three steps, first by modeling noise alone, then by identifying noise in a noise+speech signal, then by extracting the speech conditioned on the input plus the predicted noise from the previous network by using a disentanglement network. The disentanglement network includes a clean-speech model in an encoder-decoder setup. The overall system operates at the feature level (mel-spectrogram). A vocoder, trained separately on clean speech, in then used to produce time-domain samples. The authors propose to use a part of Audioset for training the noise/denoise network.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The architecture is pretty complex and relatively well motivated. For instance, the usage of RNN is still a bit surprising to me, given higher capacity models are available today, so it would be interesting to know if RNN is still the best choice for the encoder-decoder.
The block A() "mixed-signal" is not so clear to me: what is the encoder of that block - and how does it differ from the noise encoder?
Same for the Bi-LSTM at the output. My best guess is that both blocks are fine-tuned end-to-end on speech+noise from the decoder of noise and clean-speech independently. However it's a bit hard to understand from the block diagram.
The results are good and convincing, as well as extensive. However my understanding is they are mostly done on synthetic noisy data.
One interesting test would be to test on real world noisy data, with perceptual test by real users (instead of testing with real users on synthetic noisy data). That would show how well the method generalizes to real environments. Also computational complexity / real-time factor of the method would be a good metric to have.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a speech denoising network based on predicting an embedding for noise-only Mel spectrogram from a Mel spectrogram of a mixture of speech and noise. This embedding is used to "disentangle" the embedding of an encoder run on the mixture Mel spectrogram to predict the encodings of clean speech. This predicted clean speech encodings \hat{A}_C are run through a bidirectional LSTM to predict output Mel spectrogram, which is then run through a vocoder to get back to waveform. Losses to train the network include a L1 reconstruction loss for the noise-only auto-encoder, a deep feature loss between predicted clean speech embedding \hat{A}_C and ground-truth clean speech embedding A_C, and a reconstruction loss between the final predicted clean speech Mel spectrogram \hat{A}_i and the ground-truth clean speech Mel spectrogram A_i.

The approach is evaluated on noise drawn from UrbanSound8k and AudioNoiseSet (a subset of AudioSet curated by the paper to contain noise-only signals), and clean speech is drawn from AVSpeech. STOI and PESQ are used for evaluation, and the method achieves better scores compared to baselines from the literature (SEGAN, VoiceFixer, Denoiser, MetricGAN+, LSS), especially for lower SNRs. Qualitative audio demos are provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

1. I think it is interesting that the approach seems to work better (at least at lower SNRs), and I think this indicates some potential of the approach.

2. The idea of predicting noise instead of speech for speech denoising is not new (e.g. Le Roux and Hershey 2013 proposed predicting the noise from a mixture, and simply subtracting it from the input mixture; this paper should absolutely be cited):

    https://www.jonathanleroux.org/pdf/LeRoux2012ICASSP03.pdf

    I think it is interesting to see an approach use more modern deep learning tools applied to this idea, though the approach taken in this paper is a little different in that the noise is not simply subtracted from the mixture; rather, speech is predicted from the mixture and noise-only embeddings, and synthesized with a vocoder.

3. The paper promises to release their nonspeech-only version of AudioSet called AudioNoiseSet, which seems useful for the community.

### Weaknesses

1. The approach is rather complicated, involving multiple encoders, deep feature losses, and a final vocoder.

2. This premise mentioned in the abstract is absolutely incorrect:

    *"Existing approaches model speech, potentially of multiple speakers, for denoising. Such approaches have an inherent drawback as a separate model is required for each speaker."*

    Nearly all deep learning-based speech enhancement networks are trained to be speaker independent, and do not use a separate model for different speakers. Adding information about speaker identity can certainly improve performance, but speaker dependence is absolutely not necessary to get speech enhancement networks to work well.

3. I don't agree with this central motivation of this paper:

    *"Further, high variation in standards for intelligibility of speech varies with speaker, language, culture, emotion and perception...which makes generalized modelling of a speech signal challenging. To overcome this, instead of attempting to model speech, we propose to model the noise and estimate noise signal from the noisy audio, which we then utilize to obtain the denoised speech signal."*

    I would argue that "noise", i.e. all non-speech sounds, exhibits much, much more variability compared to speech signals. In fact, speech signals are some of the most structured audio sources there are, because of its characteristic shape in the time-frequency domain (e.g. sparse harmonics from voiced sounds) and predictable structure of a sequence of phonemes.

4. I found the paper title somewhat deceiving:

    *"SPEECH DENOISING BY LISTENING TO NOISE"*

    This title gave me the impression that the method was doing some kind of unsupervised or unpaired training for speech denoising. But the method uses supervised clean speech references. I would suggest adding a bit more detail to the title.

5. Thank you for providing qualitative audio demos. However, I have to say, after listening to them, I don't personally think the proposed method sounds much better than the baseline methods, even after the VF model is applied. As mentioned in the paper, the direct outputs of the method sound very robotic, and applying VF on top of this makes the voices sound hollow and hoarse. I would disagree with the paper's assessment that they are "much more understandable". I wonder if the authors should experiment with alternative architectures. Maybe instead of predicting Mel spectrograms and vocoding these, consider using a masking model in the STFT domain or learnable basis domain? You can use Mel spectrogram as the input to the networks, and have the networks predict masks for the full-resolution STFT.

Minor comments and typos

1. Multiple occurences: "melspectrogram" -> "Mel spectrogram"

2. "Audioset" -> "AudioSet"

3. "wiener" -> "Wiener"

4. Citations of classic speech enhancement technique neglects the famous MMSE and logMMSE methods by Ephraim and Malah:

    * Ephraim, Yariv, and David Malah. "Speech enhancement using a minimum-mean square error short-time spectral amplitude estimator." IEEE Transactions on acoustics, speech, and signal processing 32, no. 6 (1984): 1109-1121.

    * Ephraim, Yariv, and David Malah. "Speech enhancement using a minimum mean-square error log-spectral amplitude estimator." IEEE transactions on acoustics, speech, and signal processing 33, no. 2 (1985): 443-445.

5. "having the access clean ground truth audio." -> "having access to clean ground-truth audio."

6. "signal to onatin" -> "signal to obtain"

7. I find the {\bf a}_i notation for clean speech to be a bit weird, and potentially confusable with {\bf a}, used to indicate the mixture signal.

8. "We use a Vector Quantized VAE (VQVAE) (?) model": fix missing reference

9. "w.      GT Noise,": kind of funny to have such a long space

10. I would suggest bolding the best number within each column in the results tables.

11. You could maybe move the "Denoiser" and "w.   GT Noise" rows into Table 2, and thus get rid of Table 1.

12. "show how does our method compare" -> "show how our method compares"

13. "native english speaker" -> "native English speaker"

14. "give the resulsts" -> "give the results"

15. "of Mixed audio" -> "of mixed audio"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: mostly clear. There are a number of minor comments to address (see Minor Comments above).

Quality: okay quality. A preference user study was run, which is good. But the outputs of the model in the qualitative results sound very poor, in my opinion.

Novelty: as mentioned in weaknesses, predicting the noise from a mixture for speech denoising is not new. But this paper has some novelty in applying more modern deep learning techniques like VQ-VAE and Mel spectrogram vocoding. However, unfortunately, the combination of these components results in rather poor quality audio compared to baseline methods, even though the objective metrics improve.

Reproducibility: the paper promises to release the AudioNoiseSet. The model seems to be constructed from a number of publicly-available components and existing architectures.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposes a method of speech denoising by predicting noise from mixture audio, and using this noise prediction to enhance speech, using VQ-VAE encoder-decoders and deep speech feature loss all in the Mel spectrogram domain, and a vocoder to invert predicted Mel spectrograms back to the time domain. The method is evaluated with PESQ and STOI, achieving better scores compared to baseline methods. Qualitative audio demos are provided, but in my opinion the proposed model sounds worse than the baselines.

I think the motivation for this method is a little shaky, since the paper argues that speech is hard to model because of its variability, but I think the variability of speech is much less compared to the variability of all nonspeech sounds. There are also incorrect assertions about speaker dependence of speech denoising models.

It is interesting that the approach achieves higher STOI and PESQ metrics at lower SNRs compared to other methods, and I think indicates the potential of this approach. But more work needs to be done to fix the quality of the outputs of the model, perhaps by changing the architecture and/or loss functions to make the outputs sound less robotic.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a speech-denoising model based on noise modeling first, then conditioned on the estimated noise to predict clean speech. The proposed method is comprised of two main stages: (i) modeling the noise using a VQ-VAE model; (ii) estimating the clean signal using a bi-LSTM model. The authors additionally apply a disentanglement loss function between the representation of the clean and noise signals to further improve the results. The authors evaluated the proposed method using both objective and subjective metrics and demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:** 
1) Modeling the noise first is an interesting research direction. 
2) The proposed method provides good results under several settings. 
3) The authors provide results for various SNR levels to better reflect the advantage of the proposed method over prior work.


**Weaknesses:**
1) Although the results are interesting, there are some unfair comparisons.
2) There are some design choices in the proposed model that are not really justified and it is not clear what is their contribution to the overall model performance. 
3) Subjective tests are limited.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** clearly written

**Novelty:** somewhat novel

**Reproducibility:** partially, the authors did not provide code, but the authors said the dataset will be publicly avail
content.summary_of_the_review:
Although the paper proposed method is interesting and the results are promising, there are a few concerns that should be addressed:
1) In Table 2 and Table 3 the authors compared the proposed approach to various pre-trained baselines which were trained on different speech and noise datasets. This comparison is unfair. The authors should either use the same setup as in prior work or retrain the baseline models on their setup. For reference, the results for the denoiser only (without modeling the noise) in Table 1 already get better results than all the evaluated baselines. 
2) In Table 1, the results of the denoiser only vs. the proposed method (especially the concat) are very close. can the authors provide more info on whether these results are significant? maybe error bars? 
3) As the authors point out in the user study section, there is a mismatch between objective metrics and subjective metrics, i.e., methods that get better objective scores have metallic sounds while more natural recordings get worse objective scores. Hence, it makes a lot of sense to conduct more subjective tests, especially when considering different methods which get close to objective metrics. 
3) Another point regarding the subjective tests, the authors designed their own test, however, there is a standard subjective test IEEE ITU-T P.835 [1]. This protocol deals exactly with what the authors pointed out, overall quality, signal distortion, and background noise interference. See also the DNS challenge [2]. 
4) The authors use VQ-VAE to model the noise, can the authors mention why VQ-VAE is used and not VAE? how important the quantization process is? 

Questions and comments: 
1) Did the authors analyze the effect of the noise? meaning, how do the results change considering different types of noise?
2) In the model section, the authors said they are sampling from the VQ using Gumbel softmax. Do the authors normalize the VQ outputs? 
3) In section 4.1, there are spacing issues with the citations. 
4) Missing citation for VQ-VAE in section 3.1 

I'm willing to increase my scores in case the above points will be addressed by the authors. 

[1] I. Recommendation, “Subjective test methodology for evaluating speech communication systems that include noise suppression algorithm,” ITU-T recommendation, p. 835, 2003.
[2] Dubey, Harishchandra, et al. "Icassp 2022 deep noise suppression challenge." ICASSP 2022-2022 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP). IEEE, 2022.
